DAN-V2-CANDIDATE-010.literal_gap: Literally, “plans exist on Saturday”; in use, “I have plans on Saturday.” The person with the plans is understood from context, not stated in Korean.

DAN-V2-CANDIDATE-029.literal_gap: The default reading here is “will be busy next week.” Depending on subject and context, -(으)ㄹ 거예요 can also express a prediction or probability, such as “probably busy.”

DAN-V2-CANDIDATE-044.literal_gap: Literally, “rain comes now”; in use, “it is raining right now.” Korean uses rain as the subject rather than a dummy “it.”

DAN-V2-CANDIDATE-062.literal_gap: Literally, “because snow comes, please be careful”; in use, “it is snowing, so be careful.” Snow is the subject of 오다 (come).

DAN-V2-CANDIDATE-079.cultural_note: The warm floor can refer to ondol floor heating. The sentence itself is literal, not an idiom.

DAN-V2-CANDIDATE-086.natural_english: I'm stressed, so I have no energy.
DAN-V2-CANDIDATE-086.literal_gap: Literally, “because I receive stress, energy does not exist”; in use, “I am stressed, so I have no energy.”

DAN-V2-CANDIDATE-100.literal_gap: Literally, “I saw the test well”; in use, “I did well on the test.” 시험을 보다 means to take an exam, not look at one.

DAN-V2-CANDIDATE-137.literal_gap: 맛집 is literally “taste-house”; in use, it means a restaurant known for good food, not necessarily “the famous one.”

DAN-V2-CANDIDATE-139.cultural_note: This sentence says eating alone is fine too. The cultural term 혼밥 describes solo dining; it does not change the sentence meaning.

DAN-V2-CANDIDATE-154.cultural_note: Casual 반말: 요 and object particles are omitted. The speaker and relationship must make this register appropriate.

DAN-V2-CANDIDATE-155.literal_gap: 올렸어요 literally says “raised”; here it means “posted/uploaded.” The speaker took a selfie and then put it on social media.

DAN-V2-CANDIDATE-160.literal_gap: Literally, “if you press this, it is not okay”; in use, this expresses that pressing it is not allowed.

DAN-V2-CANDIDATE-188.literal_gap: 정 names attachment or affection accumulated through shared time. It is a single concept, not a phrase with a separate word-for-word reading; “attachment” approximates it without covering every use.

DAN-V2-CANDIDATE-204.literal_gap: Addressed to a listener, 가세요 can mean “please go.” With an honored subject, as in 선생님이 가세요, it means “the teacher is going.” The ending alone does not determine which reading is intended.
DAN-V2-CANDIDATE-204.cultural_note: This translation selects the listener-directed request reading; context can instead select an honorific statement.

DAN-V2-CANDIDATE-208.literal_gap: 되다 can mean become, work or be acceptable. 안 돼요 can therefore mean “not allowed” in a rule or refusal, “it does not work” in another context, or “no way!” as an exclamation. This translation selects the prohibition reading.

DAN-V2-CANDIDATE-213.literal_gap: In a transport context, 기사 is a driver and 님 is an honorific title. 기사님 respectfully addresses or refers to the driver; it does not mean “engineer-sir” in this use.

DAN-V2-CANDIDATE-229.literal_gap: 타다 has a concrete “ride” sense, but 썸 타다 means being in a not-yet-defined romantic or flirting stage. Here 타다 expresses experiencing that state, not riding an object called “a something.”

DAN-V2-CANDIDATE-242.literal_gap: 틀리다 means to be wrong. It should not be treated as equivalent to 다르다, “to be different”; a nonstandard use requires its own context.

DAN-V2-CANDIDATE-267.natural_english: Horses to Jeju; people to Seoul.
DAN-V2-CANDIDATE-267.literal_gap: Literally, “horses to Jeju, people to Seoul.” This proverb recommends sending each to a place suited to its prospects: Jeju for horses and Seoul for people seeking opportunity.

DAN-V2-CANDIDATE-286.literal_gap: Literally, “save the person!” In danger, this is a cry for help. It can also be exaggerated jokingly in an overwhelming situation.

DAN-V2-CANDIDATE-287.literal_gap: Literally, “the hand goes a lot”; in use, something takes a lot of care or work. 많이 describes how much the hand goes to the task, not a number of hands.

DAN-V2-CANDIDATE-290.natural_english: Running late (the dated or joking expression “Korean time”).
DAN-V2-CANDIDATE-290.literal_gap: Literally, “Korean time”; in dated or joking usage, this refers to lateness. It is not a claim that Koreans are generally late or a literal time-zone name.
